paragraphs: This checklist is for self-reflection only. It does not constitute hiring criteria, an ability rating, or a legal or regulatory conclusion. Financial Examiner roles vary considerably in authority: regulators' on-site examiners and off-site monitoring staff examine assets and liabilities, solvency, and compliance; institutional compliance and anti-money-laundering (BSA/AML) roles emphasize procedure implementation and suspicious transaction reporting; internal audit and external assurance emphasize internal controls and statement reliability; state or federal work may also involve licenses, mergers, and securities registration review. Key differences are the employing body (regulator, regulated institution, or assurance provider), statutory investigation and evidence-gathering powers, examination scope and follow-up action, and any requirement to testify in administrative proceedings or issue formal conclusions.

Test this through a paper exercise: given an entirely fictional examination package specifying the institution and its business, documents to examine, applicable regulatory requirements, examination deadlines and evidence rules, and required finding and corrective recommendation formats, write checking and evidence indexing methods, internal control and solvency points, issue characterization and supporting provisions, report structure, and correction tracking plans, marking judgments requiring internal review, statutory signatory authority, or formal proceedings.

Signals worth considering: willingness to check supporting documents individually and ground conclusions in provisions and evidence, uphold procedural fairness when challenged by examined parties, and clearly document findings and evidence. Signals calling for caution: concluding from impressions, treating examination powers as personal authority, and relaxing or tightening standards under conflicts of interest or external pressure.
This card is a career exploration reference. It does not constitute a hiring decision, ability rating, legal advice, or any regulatory conclusion.

First consider whether you can work within statutory authority and procedural constraints and organize complex materials into findings supported by legal provisions. Test this with this page's paper exercise and seven-day tasks.

Financial examiners' daily work cycles through materials, checks, characterization, and reports: obtain examined institutions' balance sheets, operating income and expenditure, loan and investment materials, and internal procedures under examination plans; check assets, liabilities, cash reserves, collateral, and institution-owned securities, reviewing audit reports and meeting records to confirm authority; characterize issues under applicable regulations, assess effects on solvency, compliance, or consumer interests, and distinguish ordinary deficiencies from major issues; prepare examination reports, issue lists, and corrective recommendations, communicate with management, track corrections, and initiate follow-up or referral procedures when necessary. Work also includes interpreting rules, training, and cross-department collaboration. O*NET additionally lists reviewing and recommending action on merger, new institution, and securities registration applications, evaluating data processing systems, planning and supervising subordinates, and training. This is occupational task scope; not every position has statutory approval or enforcement powers.

entries.answer: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Four (considerable preparation needed, SVP 7.0 to <8.0) and designates it Bright Outlook. In the education survey, about 87% report a bachelor's degree requirement, 9% a postbaccalaureate certificate, and 4% a master's degree. BLS states that typical entry-level education is an accounting-related bachelor's degree, with no related work experience required but longer-term on-the-job training under senior examiners. Common mainland Chinese requirements include accounting-, finance-, auditing-, or law-related education plus professional credentials, emphasizing regulatory knowledge, examination procedures, confidentiality, and conflicts of interest. Actual requirements depend on recruitment postings and local rules.

entries.answer: A more precise judgment is that tools will take over steps such as document extraction, summarization, provision retrieval, and working-paper drafting, while the occupation overall mainly experiences augmentation and a shift toward higher-level responsibilities. The ILO's 2023 study shows substantial differences in task exposure across occupations, with relatively lower shares of highly exposed tasks in managerial and professional occupations. Technical feasibility does not mean institutions have adopted the technology. Issue characterization, evidence-gathering scope, interview strategy, and signing conclusions require professional judgment and statutory powers. The conclusion is therefore that working methods and the focus of responsibility will change, rather than the entire occupation being replaced.
entries.question: Will AI replace this occupation?

entries.answer: No. The median is the midpoint of the wage distribution during the same statistical period, not starting pay. O*NET work-context data show predominantly regular schedules (87%); 65% work 40 hours per week and 26% more than 40 hours. Work mainly involves sitting and documents (78% sit continually or almost continually). OEWS generally excludes overtime and allowances; public-sector grade pay and market-based institutional compensation are also not directly comparable.

entries.answer: Yes, but accounting-related education and subsequent on-the-job development are usually needed. BLS states that typical entry-level education is an accounting-related bachelor's degree, with no related work experience required but longer-term on-the-job training under senior examiners. In the O*NET education survey, about 87% report a bachelor's degree requirement. Employers focus on accounting and financial analysis fundamentals, application of provisions, and working-paper standards. Common mainland Chinese requirements include accounting-, finance-, auditing-, or law-related education plus professional credentials. Statutory authority for external examinations must also be confirmed against local regulations and competent-authority rules. details: To verify tasks, work activities, work context, technology tools, interest code (CEI), and preparation level (Job Zone Four).

Tasks mainly include meeting with institutional management and external accountants and lawyers to gather evidence; recommending compliance remediation; writing examination reports and supporting schedules; addressing institutional financial soundness and problem accounts; checking balance sheets and loan documents; reviewing internal and external audit reports and meeting records; and training and guiding junior examiners (17 tasks in total).

Work context: 87% regular schedules, 13% irregular; 65% work 40 hours per week, 26% more than 40 hours; 78% sit continually or almost continually, 22% more than half the time; precision and accuracy rated extremely important by 22%, very important by 61%, and important by 13%; strict time pressure daily for 13%, more than once a week but not daily for 43%; constant contact with others for 65%, contact most of the time for 30%; 96% use email daily; about 57% encounter conflict situations at least monthly.

Technology tools mainly include compliance software, databases and query languages, document management, enterprise resource planning, financial analysis software, regulatory and case research services, and statistical and office software.

The O*NET national wage page (onetonline.org/link/localwages/13-2061.00) provides this occupation's national percentiles: annual wages of $56,230 at 10%, $70,660 at 25%, $94,160 at the median, $129,600 at 75%, and $174,200 at 90%; corresponding hourly wages are $27.04, $33.97, $45.27, $62.31, and $83.75.

subject.name: Financial Examiners
subject.summary: Inspect and supervise financial and securities institutions and financial and real estate transactions under laws and regulations: obtain balance sheets, operating income and expenditure, and loan materials to check assets and liabilities; examine internal controls involving cash reserves, collateral, and institution-owned securities; review internal and external audit reports and board and shareholder meeting records to confirm authority; recommend action on solvency, compliance, and problem accounts; prepare examination reports, issue lists, and corrective recommendations and track implementation; participate under statutory procedures in reviewing licenses, mergers, and securities registrations and make recommendations; and communicate with institutional management, external accountants, lawyers, and fellow regulators to obtain evidence.
